'''Michael Andrew Fischbach''' (born November 3, 1980) is an American chemist, microbiologist, and geneticist. He is an associate professor of Bioengineering and ChEM-H Faculty Fellow at [[Stanford University]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://profiles.stanford.edu/michael-fischbach|title=Michael Fischbach's Profile {{!}} Stanford Profiles|website=profiles.stanford.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-07-12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemh.stanford.edu/people/institute-fellows|title=Faculty Fellows {{!}} ChEM-H|website=chemh.stanford.edu|access-date=2019-07-12}}</ref> and a [[Biohub|Chan Zuckerberg Biohub]] Investigator.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.czbiohub.org/people3/investigators/|title=Investigator Program – Chan Zuckerberg Biohub|language=en-US|access-date=2019-07-12}}</ref>

== Education ==
Fischbach earned his A.B. in [[Biochemistry|Biochemical]] Sciences from [[Harvard College]] in 2003. During that time (2000–2003), he worked in Jeffrey Settleman's lab at the [[Massachusetts General Hospital]] Cancer Center on the biochemistry of oncogenic mutants of the small GTPase [[Ras superfamily|Ras]].<ref>{{cite journal | pmid = 12874011 | volume=63 | issue=14 | title=Specific biochemical inactivation of oncogenic Ras proteins by nucleoside diphosphate kinase | year=2003 | journal=Cancer Res. | pages=4089–94  | last1 = Fischbach | first1 = MA | last2 = Settleman | first2 = J}}</ref> In 2007, he earned his Ph.D. in Chemistry and Chemical Biology from Harvard University, working in [[Christopher T. Walsh]]'s laboratory at [[Harvard Medical School]] on iron acquisition in bacterial pathogens and the biochemistry of natural product biosynthesis.<ref>{{cite journal | pmid = 15598734 | doi=10.1073/pnas.0408463102 | volume=102 | issue=3 | title=In vitro characterization of IroB, a pathogen-associated C-glycosyltransferase | pmc=545562 | year=2005 | journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. | pages=571–6  | last1 = Fischbach | first1 = MA | last2 = Lin | first2 = H | last3 = Liu | first3 = DR | last4 = Walsh | first4 = CT | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Walsh | first1 = CT | last2 = Fischbach | first2 = MA | year = 2010 | title = Natural products version 2.0: connecting genes to molecules | journal = J Am Chem Soc | volume = 132 | issue = 8| pages = 2469–93 | doi = 10.1021/ja909118a | pmid = 20121095 | pmc = 2828520 | bibcode = 2010JAChS.132.2469W }}</ref>

== Career ==
Fischbach was a junior fellow in the Department of Molecular Biology at [[Massachusetts General Hospital]] (2007–2009) before joining the faculty of the [[University of California, San Francisco]] in 2009. He moved to [[Stanford University]] as an associate professor in September 2017. As a [[Chan Zuckerberg Biohub]] Investigator, Fischbach is one of eight faculty members across Stanford, UCSF, and the [[University of California, Berkeley]] leading the CZ Biohub Microbiome Initiative, launched in 2018, with the goal of understanding how the microbiota can influence human health.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2018/10/biohub-funds-new-research-efforts-microbiome-initiative.html|title=Chan Zuckerberg Biohub funds new research efforts, microbiome initiative|website=News Center|date=8 February 2017 |language=en|access-date=2019-07-12}}</ref>

Fischbach is currently a member of the scientific advisory board of NGM Biopharmaceuticals<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ngmbio.com/about/sab/|title=Scientific Advisory Board - NGM Bio|website=www.ngmbio.com|access-date=2016-01-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180720153105/http://www.ngmbio.com/about/sab/|archive-date=2018-07-20}}</ref> and a co-founder of Revolution Medicines.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://revolutionmedicines.com/team|title=Team - Revolution Medicines|website=revolutionmedicines.com}}</ref>

== Research ==
Fischbach's lab focuses on discovering and characterizing small molecules from microorganisms, with an emphasis on the human microbiome.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fischbachgroup.org/|title=Fischbach Group - Home|website=fischbachgroup.org}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Donia | first1 = MS | last2 = Fischbach | first2 = MA | year = 2015 | title = Small molecules from the human microbiota | journal = Science | volume = 349 | issue = 6246| article-number = 1254766 | doi = 10.1126/science.1254766 | pmid = 26206939 | pmc = 4641445 }}</ref>

=== Small molecules from the human microbiota ===

In 2014, Fischbach and his laboratory published a survey of biosynthetic genes in the [[Human microbiota|human microbiome]], describing the ability of human-associated microbes to produce [[thiopeptide]] antibiotics.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Donia | first1 = MS | last2 = Cimermancic | first2 = P | last3 = Schulze | first3 = CJ | last4 = Wieland Brown | first4 = LC | last5 = Martin | first5 = J | last6 = Mitreva | first6 = M | last7 = Clardy | first7 = J | last8 = Linington | first8 = RG | last9 = Fischbach | first9 = MA | year = 2014 | title = A systematic analysis of biosynthetic gene clusters in the human microbiome reveals a common family of antibiotics | journal = Cell | volume = 158 | issue = 6| pages = 1402–14 | doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2014.08.032 | pmid = 25215495 | pmc = 4164201 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/09/11/health/mining-for-antibiotics-right-under-our-noses.html|title=Mining for Antibiotics, Right Under Our Noses|date=2014-09-11|work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://time.com/3341260/diy-drugs-antibiotics-could-soon-be-made-out-of-your-own-bacteria/|title=DIY Drugs: Antibiotics Could Soon Be Made Out of Your Own Bacteria|last=Park|first=Alice|date=2014-09-12|magazine=Time|language=en-us|access-date=2018-04-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21618674-humanitys-bacterial-companions-are-good-place-look-new-drugs-set|title=Set a thief... Humanity's bacterial companions are a good place to look for new drugs|date=2014-09-20|newspaper=The Economist|language=en|access-date=2018-04-26}}</ref>  The Fischbach lab discovered that the gut commensal Bacteroides fragilis produces the immune modulatory sphingolipid alpha-galactosylceramide,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Wieland Brown | first1 = LC | author-link6 = Mitchell Kronenberg | last2 = Penaranda | first2 = C | last3 = Kashyap | first3 = PC | last4 = Williams | first4 = BB | last5 = Clardy | first5 = J | last6 = Kronenberg | first6 = M | last7 = Sonnenburg | first7 = JL | last8 = Comstock | first8 = LE | last9 = Bluestone | first9 = JA | last10 = Fischbach | first10 = MA | date = Jul 2013 | title = Production of α-galactosylceramide by a prominent member of the human gut microbiota | journal = PLOS Biol | volume = 11 | issue = 7| article-number = e1001610 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pbio.1001610 | doi-access = free | pmid = 23874157 | pmc = 3712910 }}</ref> showed that the production of neurotransmitters is common among commensal gut bacteria,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Williams | first1 = BB | last2 = Van Benschoten | first2 = AH | last3 = Cimermancic | first3 = P | last4 = Donia | first4 = MS | last5 = Zimmermann | first5 = M | last6 = Taketani | first6 = M | last7 = Ishihara | first7 = A | last8 = Kashyap | first8 = PC | last9 = Fraser | first9 = JS | last10 = Fischbach | first10 = MA | date = Oct 2014 | title = Discovery and characterization of gut microbiota decarboxylases that can produce the neurotransmitter tryptamine | journal = Cell Host Microbe | volume = 16 | issue = 4| pages = 495–503 | doi = 10.1016/j.chom.2014.09.001 | pmid = 25263219 | pmc = 4260654 }}</ref> and discovered the biosynthetic pathway for a common class of [[bile acid]]s produced by gut bacteria.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Devlin | first1 = AS | last2 = Fischbach | first2 = MA | date = Sep 2015 | title = A biosynthetic pathway for a prominent class of microbiota-derived bile acids | journal = Nat Chem Biol | volume = 11 | issue = 9| pages = 685–90 | doi = 10.1038/nchembio.1864 | pmid = 26192599 | pmc = 4543561 }}</ref>

=== Computational approaches to natural product discovery ===

Fischbach's lab developed an algorithm, ClusterFinder, that automates the process of identifying biosynthetic genes for small molecules in bacterial genome sequences.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Cimermancic | first1 = P | last2 = Medema | first2 = MH | last3 = Claesen | first3 = J | last4 = Kurita | first4 = K | last5 = Wieland Brown | first5 = LC | last6 = Mavrommatis | first6 = K | last7 = Pati | first7 = A | last8 = Godfrey | first8 = PA | last9 = Koehrsen | first9 = M | last10 = Clardy | first10 = J | last11 = Birren | first11 = BW | last12 = Takano | first12 = E | last13 = Sali | first13 = A | last14 = Linington | first14 = RG | last15 = Fischbach | first15 = MA | year = 2014 | title = Insights into secondary metabolism from a global analysis of prokaryotic biosynthetic gene clusters | journal = Cell | volume = 158 | issue = 2| pages = 412–21 | doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2014.06.034 | pmid = 25036635 | pmc = 4123684 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Medema | first1 = MH | last2 = Fischbach | first2 = MA | date = Sep 2015 | title = Computational approaches to natural product discovery | url = | journal = Nat Chem Biol | volume = 11 | issue = 9| pages = 639–48 | doi = 10.1038/nchembio.1884 | pmid = 26284671 | pmc = 5024737 }}</ref> With Marnix Medema, he co-developed a second algorithm for identifying biosynthetic gene clusters, antiSMASH,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://antismash.secondarymetabolites.org/|title=antiSMASH bacterial version|website=antismash.secondarymetabolites.org}}</ref> with which ClusterFinder has been merged.

=== Engineered Bacteria Therapeutics ===
Fischbach's team has made significant strides in engineering commensal bacteria for therapeutic purposes. They transformed the ubiquitous skin bacterium [[Staphylococcus]] epidermidis into a topical vaccine platform.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bousbaine |first1=Djenet |last2=Bauman |first2=Katherine D. |last3=Chen |first3=Y. Erin |last4=Lalgudi |first4=Pranav V. |last5=Nguyen |first5=Tam T. D. |last6=Swenson |first6=Joyce M. |last7=Yu |first7=Victor K. |last8=Tsang |first8=Eunice |last9=Conlan |first9=Sean |last10=Li |first10=David B. |last11=Jbara |first11=Amina |last12=Zhao |first12=Aishan |last13=Naziripour |first13=Arash |last14=Veinbachs |first14=Alessandra |last15=Lee |first15=Yu E. |date=2024-12-11 |title=Discovery and engineering of the antibody response to a prominent skin commensal |journal=Nature |volume=638 |issue=8052 |language=en |pages=1054–1064 |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-08489-4 |pmid=39662508 |issn=1476-4687|pmc=12045117 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Stanford scientists transform ubiquitous skin bacterium into a topical vaccine |url=https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2024/12/skin-bacteria-vaccine.html |access-date=2025-01-21 |website=med.stanford.edu |date=11 December 2024 |language=en-US}}</ref> This approach generated potent, durable, and specific antibody responses in mice, potentially offering a new method for vaccine delivery.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Jeong-Mi |last2=Sage |first2=Peter T. |date=2024-12-19 |title=Skin in the game — locally made antibodies fight resident bacteria |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-024-04205-4 |journal=Nature |volume=638 |issue=8052 |pages=894–896 |language=en |doi=10.1038/d41586-024-04205-4 |pmid=39702488 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 2023, his postdoc Erin Chen led an effort to engineer skin bacteria  to induce antitumor [[T cell]] responses against melanoma, highlighting the potential of the skin microbiome in cancer immunotherapy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Y. Erin |last2=Bousbaine |first2=Djenet |last3=Veinbachs |first3=Alessandra |last4=Atabakhsh |first4=Katayoon |last5=Dimas |first5=Alex |last6=Yu |first6=Victor K. |last7=Zhao |first7=Aishan |last8=Enright |first8=Nora J. |last9=Nagashima |first9=Kazuki |last10=Belkaid |first10=Yasmine |last11=Fischbach |first11=Michael A. |date=2023-04-14 |title=Engineered skin bacteria induce antitumor T cell responses against melanoma |journal=Science |volume=380 |issue=6641 |pages=203–210 |doi=10.1126/science.abp9563|pmid=37053311 |bibcode=2023Sci...380..203C |pmc=12356174 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Researchers use skin-colonizing bacteria to create a topical cancer therapy in mice |url=https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2023/04/cancer-bacteria.html |access-date=2025-01-21 |website=News Center |date=12 April 2023 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Fischbach is married to [[Elizabeth Sattely]], Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at Stanford.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://profiles.stanford.edu/elizabeth-sattely|title=Elizabeth Sattely's Profile {{!}} Stanford Profiles|website=profiles.stanford.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-07-12}}</ref>
